Doctor:  Can you describe the double vision—does it happen all the time or only when looking in certain directions?  
Doctor:  Has the weakness in your arms and legs been getting worse over time or is it constant?  
Doctor:  Have you noticed any changes in your balance or coordination, like difficulty walking?

The double vision usually occurs when I look up or down, but not when I look straight ahead. The weakness in my arms and legs feels worse after climbing stairs or doing other activities, but it gets better if I rest for a while. I haven’t noticed any changes in balance or coordination, and I don’t have tingling or numbness—just the weakness and fatigue.

Doctor:  Is the double vision accompanied by any eye movement issues, such as difficulty tracking objects?

I haven’t had any infections or fevers before the symptoms started, and I don’t have a family history of neurological disorders. The weakness feels symmetrical, affecting both arms and both legs equally.

The symptoms started gradually about a month ago, slowly worsening with activity.

My double vision seems to be triggered by fatigue—like after climbing stairs or doing more work with my hands.

The double vision tends to happen more after I’ve been using my eyes for a long time, like when working on the computer for a while.
